paras: The whitecapping of Joe Shively and the Stevens women was a night attack in which white men broke into a house at Bloomington, Indiana, early on April 26, 1903, and whipped Joe Shively, a Black man, and white women of the Stevens family. Governor Durbin threatened to have the State University moved unless the attackers were punished, which made the case a statewide story. Seven men were arrested, but the prosecution stalled, and by October Shively was said to have repudiated his account.

Shively shared a double tenement with a white widow, Sarah Stevens, and her daughters, though reports differ on the women's names and ages. The Indianapolis Journal wrote that the house "has borne a bad reputation" and that Shively had been living there "on terms of perfect equality with the white women"; a wire version spoke of rumors of "improper relations."

At about one o'clock in the morning the men forced their way in. According to the Journal, twelve masked men tied Shively to a sapling in a nearby grove and lashed him about fifty times, then stripped two Stevens women and Shively's sister to the waist and whipped them "until the blood ran." The wire version counted thirty-eight men and said Shively, aged fifty, was whipped with barbed wire and hit in the eye with brass knuckles. Shively was ordered to leave the county, and the women were also told to go.

On April 27 Governor Durbin wrote to Sheriff Thrasher and said he would propose to the Legislature "the removal of the State University from a community that permits it to be disgraced." The sheriff replied that he had been told the affair was "only a row in a house of bad repute." Prosecutor R. G. Miller and Mayor Dunn then held a court of inquiry that heard about thirty witnesses, and on May 1 seven men, among them Policeman William Shinn, were arrested and released on bond. Shinn was reported to have been identified by three of the four victims.

Shively soon wrote to the Governor for protection, reporting that he had been given fifteen days to leave town "on penalty of death." In June the indictments were quashed because they omitted "Monroe county," the men were rearrested, and the new charges were challenged in turn. In October the Journal reported that Shively was said to have sworn he had not been whipped and did not recognize the accused. New affidavits on October 30 added two Branhams and dropped Shinn, and no report of a trial or verdict appears in the coverage.

The Journal's first report said local "sentiment seems to be with the unknown visitors to the Stevens home." Out-of-state papers ran the wire under headlines about the white women, such as "Girl Whipped With Barbed Wire" in the New-York Tribune and "Whitecaps Whip Women" in the New York Sun, and called Shively "a negro." After the Governor intervened, the Bloomington Daily Telephone, reprinted in the Journal, insisted "It was not what people know as 'whitecapping.'"

The Black press covered the case in short items. A Bloomington correspondent told the Western World that masked men had whipped two white girls and "the colored man with barbed wire." The Indianapolis Freeman backed the Governor and, after Shively's appeal, wrote that "If Shively has committed a crime he should be tried for it." The Cleveland Gazette stressed that the intimacy was only "CLAIMED" and used the case to call for mob-violence laws like Ohio's, while the Professional World reprinted the wire.

The first reports described twelve masked citizens "of excellent character," and the wire described thirty-eight men, masked in some versions and unmasked in others. The Telephone and the court of inquiry described drunken, unmasked men who had frequented the house and attacked when the women refused them admission, and the Plymouth Tribune reported that the victims called the attackers "bums, toughs and hangers-on about the saloons." Shively's recantation was reported secondhand, after his report of the death threat.

reader.title: Whitecapping of Joe Shively and the Stevens women
bases: A band of men broke into a house at night, whipped a Black man and white women, and ordered them out of the county, and the papers and the Governor called it whitecapping (A1, A3, A4), though the local Daily Telephone denied it was whitecapping (A7).

The night whipping is reported independently by the Indianapolis Journal's Bloomington report, the wire, a Black-press correspondent, the local Daily Telephone and the court of inquiry with neighbor witnesses (A1, A2, A7, A9, A17); the one denial is a secondhand October report that Shively had sworn he was not whipped (A23).

accounts.label: Indianapolis Journal first report
accounts.gist: Twelve masked men, believed to be citizens 'of excellent character', whipped Shively, his sister and two white women for living together 'on terms of perfect equality'; local sentiment favored the mob.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Thirty-eight men (masked or unmasked by version) broke in, whipped Shively and the older girl with barbed wire and the younger with switches, and hit Shively with brass knuckles; many were recognized.

accounts.label: Black correspondent (Western World)
accounts.gist: A few masked men broke into a house and whipped two white girls and a colored man, the man with barbed wire.

accounts.label: Daily Telephone and local citizens
accounts.gist: Unmasked drunken rowdies who had frequented the house broke in after being refused admission; it was a row at a questionable place, not whitecapping.

accounts.label: Victims (via court of inquiry)
accounts.gist: The mob was drunken 'bums, toughs and hangers-on about the saloons' whom the victims recognized; Shively and others identified Policeman Shinn.

accounts.label: Shively's letter to the Governor
accounts.gist: He had been given fifteen days to leave on penalty of death and named the man who threatened him.

accounts.label: Defense (reported)
accounts.gist: Shively was said to have sworn that he was not whipped and recognized none of the accused.

framing.detail: The Indianapolis Journal's first report gave the mob's racial reason without challenge and said 'sentiment seems to be with the unknown visitors', then gave Governor Durbin's denunciation front-page play.
Out-of-state papers ran the wire under headlines on whipped white women and barbed wire ('Girl Whipped With Barbed Wire', 'Whitecaps Whip Women').
The Bloomington Daily Telephone, reprinted in the Journal, called the attack an offense to be punished but denied it was 'whitecapping' and defended the town's citizens.
The Western World's correspondent gave a three-line factual report.
The Indianapolis Freeman backed the Governor and said Shively should be tried if he had committed a crime, and otherwise left alone.
The Cleveland Gazette stressed that intimacy was only 'CLAIMED' and used the case to call for mob-violence laws.
The Professional World reprinted the wire as 'Whitecappers Whip Girls'.
